newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's CSU wants limit on foreign job-seekers.
newsitem.headline: Germany's CSU wants limit on foreign job-seekers.

text.p: Germany's conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) said on Tuesday it would consider calling for tougher limits on foreigners seeking work, to get more Germans into jobs and head off resentment of foreigners.

A paper to be discussed at a party meeting next month calls for people from outside the European Union living in Germany to wait five years before they can work, said a spokesman for the CSU, a junior partner in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition.

The move come shortly after CSU parliamentary leader Michael Glos said there were too many immigrants in the country taking jobs away from German workers, and that taxpayers were fed up with the high costs of supporting foreigners.
The paper has yet to become party policy and is even further from getting the backing of Kohl's centre-right Christian Democrats (CDU) or the liberal Free Democrats in the government.

But it appeared to mark a new effort by the most right-wing of Germany's mainstream parties to erode taboos about the treatment of foreigners in Germany, still a sensitive issue because of the organised racism perpetrated by the Nazis.
A spokesman for the CSU's parliamentary group said the paper put forward the view that immigration was an increasingly urgent problem with high welfare costs.
It said there was a risk of increased racism as this immigration added to unemployment, which already stands at post-war record levels around four million.
The daily Bild said the draft paper also suggested that German nationals should be given preferential treatment by labour offices.

Glos told Monday's news weekly Der Spiegel Germany could "no longer tolerate the fact that millions of our own citizens are unemployed, but at the same time more than one million foreigners are given work permits in Germany every year".

German politicians rarely speak out so directly against foreigners for fear of laying themselves open to accusations of racism, especially since more than 30 people died in a three-year wave of anti-foreigner violence in the early 1990s.
About nine percent of Germany's population of 81 million are foreign nationals.
